items.titel: Science Friction: An Argument for More Sex in Sci-Fi
items.anriss: For centuries, sailors enduring months-long voyages would gaze out at sea mammals sunning themselves and think the thought as old as thought itself: ​ “Would.” ​ Even famously reliable Christopher Columbus—[jerkoff hand motion]—claims in …

absaetze.t: Adam Peterson Makes the Case for Sexual Desire in Space
This first appeared in Lit Hub’s Craft of Writing newsletter—sign up here.
Article continues after advertisement

For centuries, sailors enduring months-long voyages would gaze out at sea mammals sunning themselves and think the thought as old as thought itself: ​ “Would.” ​ Even famously reliable Christopher Columbus—[jerkoff hand motion]—claims in his journal to have seen mermaids (almost certainly half-ton, gray-skinned manatees) though the legend goes much further back. Seductive aquatic creatures luring sailors to a watery death is a story that pretty much originated with sailing itself. Isolate men on a ship, send them into a vast and vacant sea, and, well, they’re going to see some stuff. Anyone watching is going to see some stuff. ​ Some stuff is going to happen. ​ This frustrated, misdirected desire isn’t something unique to sailors or men, and it’s not something that went away with better vision care. Being bored and horny is pretty much the human condition—one exacerbated by isolation and distance and anything else that removes us from the people and distractions we’ve assembled in our lives to forget this fact for as long as we can. ​ Which is why it’s odd that in our literature when we imagine the most extreme voyages we can—departing our planet and heading out into the stars—sexual desire too often gets left on Earth, and the most alien thing to be found can be the human characters. ​ Why would they possibly touch each other when there’s all this math to do? ​ In many science fiction novels, desire is treated as a technology too primitive for future worlds of warp drives and laser blasters. A thing humanity must evolve beyond (or at least learn to control) to reach our highest destiny as galaxy conquering space lords or whatever.

That’s maybe even understandable because, at least as far as NASA is willing to admit, no one has ever had sex in space. The question of what it would even look like is an entire field of study that actually does involve a fair amount of technological problem solving. But in fictional worlds with artificial gravity, there’s no reason to treat love as something that needs a few more rounds of testing before it’s launch-ready. ​ Even those canonical sci-fi writers who do feature sex in their works often approach it this way. Characters can’t just have sex but have to have something more like FutureSex™. Think Iain M. Banks and his gender switching, animal hybrids in Consider Phlebas or the time-hopping Shrike-screwing soldier in Dan Simmon’s Hyperion. You can imagine the engineers hiding in the closet taking notes on what the next release patch will fix. ​ So the sex that does occur in science fiction is commonly a little scary and a lot weird and arriving with more than a touch of an author’s particular kinks. Nothing inherently wrong with that, of course, but in the unfortunately male dominated world of sci-fi, it probably goes a long way toward explaining some of what’s happening here.

Science fiction is a genre of not only exploration but of explanation. Wish fulfillment, sure, but if the wishes came with an instruction manual. Here’s all this fantastic stuff, but first let me give you the terms and conditions. Stories of great speed told slowly. This creates a natural tension with sexual desire, which is by nature inexplicable. Because science fiction writers aren’t exactly wrong in recognizing sex as an older, stranger technology. Primal and irrational but also inevitable and fixed. Our first and forever.
But it doesn’t fit neatly into stories that value the science over the fiction.

Writing about love and sex also involves wish fulfillment, of course, but only after a whole lot more wish denial. Romance is slow stories told fast. And so the romantasy genre feels inevitable when sexual desire is more magic than logic, but that doesn’t mean the equivalent in science fiction is impossible. There’s a natural lane here for understanding what lust looks like in the vacuum of space. We just have to go back to those sailors trapped exploring their own era’s final frontier.
The sea was empty, so they saw sex. Because bored. Because horny.

And that’s as natural at lightspeed as it is sailing around the Mediterranean. No distance will separate us from our humanity. We won’t reject our desires simply because no amount of data can—or should—explain them. We were bored and horny when we left our first cave, and we’ll be bored and horny when we leave this planet, whatever we find. Because while we might be in awe of our sci-fi worlds, to our characters they’re as unremarkable as a Tuesday night at Applebees. Another thing to be endured before they get another chance to get off.
It’s human nature then, now, and always.

No one is arguing our heroes should look out the windows of their starship and see space mermaids, but they should at least recognize a human face reflected in the glass. They should still take a moment between outrunning galactic empires or slaughtering alien civilizations to remember they have bodies. And having one of those is as strange and terrifying as anything else in the universe.

Once writers start from that understanding, sci-mantasy (Science-friction? No? Fine.) will pretty much take care of itself. Because in space, where nothing is alive, there’s only one way to assure ourselves that we are. And it’s not math.
Any Time but This Time by Adam Peterson is available via Mad Creek Books.

absaetze.t: A young adult man with closely cropped dark brown hair sits in a wheelchair in a dimly lit room, facing a computer screen on which a simple phrase is typed out: “How are you ­today?” Underneath the question on the screen, three dots appear—similar to the ones messaging apps use to signal that your conversation partner is composing a response—and flash with anticipation. One by one, new words materialize: “I am very good.”

At first glance, this brief conversation doesn’t seem particularly special, but the man’s situation is anything but ordinary. On top of his head is a small box, about one inch square in size, connected to a circular portal in his skull about the size of a nickel. Protruding from the box is a thin black cable. The man, who goes by the nickname Pancho, is para­lyzed and unable to speak, but a BCI rec­ords brain waves from the part of his cortex that is responsible for generating speech, the vocal motor cortex, and translates them into words on the computer screen.

In 2003, at the age of twenty, Pancho experienced a devastating brainstem stroke while recovering from a car accident and major surgery. After a week in a coma, he woke up para­lyzed and unable to speak. The connections between his brain and his vocal muscles disrupted by the stroke, he couldn’t even make sounds as he cried.

For years, Pancho’s main method of verbal communication relied on a pointer attached to a baseball cap. He’d use the limited mobility that remained in his neck to move his head forward and down to tap keys on a computer screen, one at a time. Spelling out words like this enabled him to communicate, albeit at the agonizingly slow pace of five words per minute. “I always was told by doctors that I had zero chance of getting better,” he wrote in a 2021 interview. But in recent years, a groundbreaking brain implant and a research collaboration with scientists at the University of California, San Francisco has been, for Pancho, “very much like getting a second chance to talk again.”

The lab of neurosurgeon and scientist Edward Chang builds technologies that help paralyzed people like Pancho recover their ability to communicate by translating their brain activity into language. The Chang lab’s speech prosthesis project has incorporated many of the elements of the neuroscience tool kit we’ve discussed in other chapters; for example, like other BCIs, it uses precise e-phys recordings from specific parts of the brain that are important for generating behaviors. Before working with Pancho, Chang and his colleagues spent over a decade studying the basic neurobiology of speech in the human brain using similar recordings from non-paralyzed subjects. In brain-mapping studies that recalled Wilder Penfield’s pioneering work, his team steadily uncovered fundamental principles of how speech is represented by neural activity. Pancho’s implant, a delicate array of electrodes spread over a flat, flexible rectangular device like a business card, is placed on the surface of his vocal motor cortex, which governs speech production. Wire-thin cables protruding from the implant exit Pancho’s skull through the coin-sized opening. These electrode arrays, which contain anywhere from 128 to just over 200 separate electrodes, record the collective activity of many neurons and send the neural waveforms to a computer for analysis.
These are not the fever dreams of a tech CEO; they are the result of decades of ingenuity and perseverance in the lab and in the clinic.

The BCI relies on a phenomenon called persistent somatotopy, which is when a stroke or other injury prevents outgoing neural signals from the brain to the body (such as the mouth and tongue), but the cortical neurons that generate those signals are still functioning properly. Consequently, BCIs can read out the muscle movements these patients try to make. The idea is that, although their paralysis blocks the neural signals from reaching their muscles, those signals are still generated in the brain. In Pancho’s case, Chang and his team had no way of knowing what those signals would be like, and to what degree they would represent language with fidelity after sixteen years of paralysis (Pancho was thirty-six at the start of his collaboration with Chang).

Thankfully, Pancho’s vocal motor cortex still shows a healthy amount of neural activity, but even in ideal circumstances, it’s no small feat to translate those neural impulses to language. Here is where A.I. comes in. A model called an artificial neural network looks for patterns in the brain activity associated with phonemes, or the auditory building blocks of words, that the user reads on a screen—a feat that A.I. accomplishes much more quickly and accurately than a human data analyst. Whereas previous models matched neural activity to a limited vocabulary of words, this updated A.I. model is able to dramatically expand patients’ vocabularies by focusing on phonemes instead. The set of phonemes the model can recognize from brain activity, when combined in differ­ent ways to create differ­ent words, covers a vocabulary that amounts to nearly 90 ­percent of the ­English language.

Over time, an individual’s A.I. model improves at matching their neural activity to the words they read on a screen and focus intently on trying to say. Eventually, even when the person tries to say something spontaneously—­that is, from their own mind rather than when prompted—­the A.I. can predict their words.

Over the past twenty years or so, para­lyzed ­people have been able to communicate verbally using BCIs or other devices, but the process remained slow. For example, one type of BCI recorded signals from a part of the motor cortex that let the user control the movement of a cursor on a screen. Moving it across an array of letters laid out like a keyboard, that user could type out words one letter at a time. Another device tracked its user’s eye movements, which are retained in otherwise para­lyzed ­people who have a brainstem disorder called “locked-in syndrome,” as they looked at individual letters. Here, too, words needed to be typed out one letter at a time—not ideal for speed. ­These types of devices could only read out about 10 words per minute—double the speed of Pancho’s pointer-­on-­a-baseball-­cap technique, but a long way from the 120 to 150 words per minute characteristic of natu­ral speech. The recent BCI from Chang’s team enables a word output of almost 80 words per minute.

However, speech is more than just phonemes and words. Though it’s easy to take this for granted in an age when so much communication takes place through text, speech is biologically linked to facial expression and tone of voice. ­These nonverbal characteristics are impor­tant for conveying emotion, and para­lyzed ­people unable to move their facial muscles lose their ability to communicate in this critical dimension. Recognizing this, Chang’s team designed their BCI and A.I. models to read and interpret the activity in the vocal motor regions of the brain to restore the personalized sound of someone’s voice and the facial expressions that match their speech. Though not yet able to reanimate a paralyzed person’s real face, these technologies allow them to communicate with speech and facial expressions via a humanlike avatar on a screen.
The patient at the center of this research is a woman named Ann who experienced a devastating stroke while playing volleyball with friends on a sunny day when she was only thirty years old.

Rather than just being displayed on a screen, Ann’s words, predicted by the recordings from her BCI, are “spoken” by a computer-generated avatar of a woman whose voice sounds remarkably like Ann’s used to. Creating a synthetic voice from recordings is a process referred to as “voice banking.” Patients with a neurodegenerative disease, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, or Lou Gehrig’s disease), can preserve a library of vocal recordings before their condition progresses and impacts their speech. Later, the recordings can be used to create more realistic-sounding speech from a BCI like Ann’s. In her case, the avatar’s voice was generated based on recordings taken from before her stroke, including her wedding speech captured on video.

The Chang lab’s A.I. model also enables Ann to communicate nonverbally by animating the facial movements of her avatar. This most recent development was driven by another state-of-the-art feature of her speech BCI. The human vocal motor cortex comprises subregions that drive movements in discrete parts of the vocal tract, such as the tongue, jaw, and lips. Ann’s BCI translates neural activity into the avatar’s speech by focusing not on words or even phonemes, but on movements of these vocal muscles. By breaking speech down into the muscular components of individual phonemes, the team was able to re-create both speech and the individual elements of facial expression that were sent to the avatar animation. This allows Ann’s BCI to translate neural activity into facial expressions conveying emotion—in fact, with or without accompanying speech.

In their 2023 Nature paper about Ann’s BCI, the research team noted that the A.I. model made mistakes about a quarter of the time, though sentences were often still comprehensible when several of the component words were incorrect. However, as technology continues to improve, the team hopes to minimize errors and facilitate real-time communication between paralyzed patients and the people around them. One example of this is the recent development of a bilingual speech prosthesis that can seamlessly translate neural signals into English or Spanish. To accomplish this, researchers used transfer learning—the same technique used by Mackenzie Mathis to enable DeepLabCut to recognize and track body parts from lab videos. Because different languages might consist of different vocabularies but still share phonemes, their A.I. model applied the neural data recorded in one language to learn the other.

When we think about brain implants and A.I. avatars communicating with humans, we can imagine dystopian, sinister, or purely commercial applications: an A.I. with a humanlike avatar meant to dupe us or a brain implant that reads out our neural activity to queue up the next song on our morning drive playlist. Even neuroscientists, toiling away in the lab on our esoteric experiments, might admit these applications can sound cool. But ultimately, this is not what neural circuits research is all about. Pancho and Ann, on the other hand, are two real examples of how this technology—and the neural circuits research that drives it—is actually being used to help patients. These are not the fever dreams of a tech CEO; they are the result of decades of ingenuity and perseverance in the lab and in the clinic, not to mention millions of dollars in public funding.

Funding institutions like the NIH often publicize their “moonshots,” like the Human Genome Project or the BRAIN Initiative, with splashy press conferences and websites. These moonshot projects emphasize nonlinear, long-term scientific advancement, often without a specific cure or even a tangible goal in mind. But what motivates individual scientists to do basic research is often something more personal. Every day, neuroscience labs in the United States and across the world are humming along, focused on a different kind of moonshot—the moonshots that patients with brain disorders and injuries wish for themselves and their loved ones: one more milestone for a baby with cerebral palsy, or one more birthday for a grandmother with Alzheimer’s.
Though science is imperfect and fallible by definition, I think people would feel more trust if they understood a bit more about how it is done, who does it, and why.

« No Dior, no Dietrich » ! La formule, que la maison imprime sur sacs et tee-shirts, serait née d’un ultimatum, sur le tournage du Grand Alibi d’Hitchcock, lancé par l’actrice Marlene Dietrich qui voulait être habillée de la tête aux pieds par le couturier. Sylvain Chomet, l’enchanteur des Triplettes de Belleville et de Marcel et Monsieur Pagnol en a fait un joli conte à déballer dès maintenant.
Il était une fois… une robe

Le trait à la main ressuscite avec tendresse Monsieur Dior par une nuit d’hiver 1949. Au bout du fil, Hollywood s’affole : Marlene devait tourner en noir et blanc mais le film passe finalement à la couleur. Il lui faut, sur-le-champ, une robe éclatante !

Cette fable narrée par Robert Pattinson, égérie de la saga Twilight, convoque une constellation de stars. Louis Garrel s’est glissé dans la voix du couturier, Camille Cottin prête son timbre de velours à la diva Dietrich. Josh O’Connor s’est mué en chaise facétieuse et iconique de la maison, tandis que les actrices Nine d’Urso, Nadia Tereszkiewicz et Greta Lee papillonnent en couturières ailées (Paulette, Yvonne et Marguerite), clin d’œil au surnom d’« abeilles » que Christian Dior donnait à ses assistantes aux mains d’or.
Rihanna en haut du sapin

« Shine, Bright » ! Miracle de Noël, juchée sur un sapin, la chanteuse Rihanna, en étoile porte-bonheur (un fétiche de Monsieur Dior), souffle l’idée salvatrice au créateur. Ainsi par une divine nuit naît la robe « Junon », merveilleuse cascade de tulle pailleté de bleu et de vert. Seule entorse à cette belle histoire : Dietrich ne l’a jamais portée. Les contes de fées servent à rêver !
